newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-MGM Atlantic City project may lag.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-MGM Atlantic City project may lag.

text.p: MGM Grand Inc's President, Chief Operating Officer and Chief Financial Officer Alex Yemenidjian said the company may not be able to meet its initial goal of breaking ground on an Atlantic City, N.J., hotel/casino by the end of 1997.

"Whether or not we can accomplish that remains to be seen," he told Reuters in an interview at the Montgomery Securities Hospitality Conference in New York, citing constraints on obtaining the five acres or so of additional pieces of land that the company might require.

Yemenidjian said the city authorities had started the paperwork that could lead to condemnation of the required land, which MGM could then buy. He said he saw the Atlantic City project being completed by the year 2000.
MGM has said it plans to build a $700 million hotel casino in Atlantic City on over 30 acres fronting the Boardwalk, with construction taking 24 to 30 months after groundbreaking.

Yemenidjian also that the company had almost finished the first phase of its renovations at its flagship property MGM Grand Hotel/Casino in Las Vegas, and would probably start the second phase this month.

"Phase Two we would start probably this February, this month," he said. He also said that while the company had budgeted $250 million for the entire project, "it's possible it could cost more than that."

The second phase in the planned transformation of the complex into "The City of Entertainment" includes work on its Lion Entry. Yemenidjian said he does not see the work impeding traffic because "a lot of the construction that we're going to do is really outside the traffic area."
Phase Three is targeted to take place in the first half of 1998 and the final fourth phase in the last half, he said.

He said the company presently understood that the city of Detroit -- where MGM hopes to open a casino -- intended to issue a "request-for-proposal" in late February, and MGM is deciding whether to bid separately or team up with one of the two parties prelicensed there.
Either way, he said, "We will aggressively pursue the license."
The two parties are 400 Monroe Associates, which is in the restaurant/hotel business in Detroit, and a group called Atwater Group.
Yemenidjian said he hoped the selection process would be completed by late summer or early fall so that a temporary facility could be opened by early 1998 or late 1997.
He declined to say how much MGM planned to spend on Detroit, or the proposed size of the facility, saying such projections were "premature."

Earlier, in his presentation, Yemenidjian had said the company had set a goal of increasing its operating cash flow or EBITDA (earnings before interest expense, tax, depreciation and amortization) from $250 million in 1996 to over $500 million by the time Atlantic City was opened.
This projection was based on properties owned or in the pipeline.

"If we actually are successful in one of the three licenses in Detroit, we might end up trippling our EBITDA by the time both Detroit and Atlantic City are open," he told Reuters. In November, Detroit voters passed a law allowing three gambling licenses there, making it one of the first major markets to open in years.

Asked whether the company saw any acquisitions on the horizon, Yemenidjian said nothing could be ruled out but added, "We don't see anything out there at the moment that is properly priced. I think everything out there is overpriced."

He said MGM's partnership with Primadonna Resorts Inc, with which it owns the recently opened New York-New York Hotel/Casino in Las Vegas, was working well and "would hopefully continue into the long run."
At this point, he said, "I don't think either party is a seller," referring to the option either party has of making a bid for the other's stake six months after the opening.
"New York-New York has a very good chance of being the property with the highest profit margin on the Strip," he said.
((--New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610))
